segments.title: Historical context, revision, and primary sources
segments.body: Historical actors need to be understood in the terms available to them, even when their actions remain wrong. Historians often revise established accounts because newly discovered primary sources allow a more accurate explanation. Additional evidence can turn a simple cause-and-effect account into a chain of interacting events. The purpose of that complexity is to understand what happened more clearly, rather than to make the story complicated for its own sake.

evidence.note: Understanding historical actors on their own terms differs from approving their actions; additional primary sources can reveal a more complex causal chain and require revision.

segments.summary: Historical context means examining what people thought in their own time without treating explanation as approval, while new primary sources can revise accounts of causation.

segments.title: USS Texas and the weight of a 14-inch broadside
segments.body: A viewer praises the US 14-inch gun and puts its Mark 16 shell about 300 pounds below the German 15-inch shell in the comparison. Texas's ten guns give the comparison its force: shell weight and gun count both affect the weight of a broadside. A later comment corrects an assumption that Texas carried only 12-inch guns. The surrounding jokes about Texas defying physics express admiration for the ship without establishing a technical advantage over another battleship.

evidence.note: A viewer compares the US 14-inch Mark 16 shell with a German 15-inch shell and cites Texas's ten guns. The reply adds humorous praise rather than a technical assessment of a battle.
A later viewer acknowledges having mistaken Texas's armament for 12-inch guns, and the reply repeats the 14-inch calibre.

segments.summary: A viewer compares Texas's ten 14-inch guns and Mark 16 shells with German 15-inch armament, drawing attention to shell weight and gun count.

segments.title: Illustrious keeps serving despite reduced speed
segments.body: An imagined fleet of unusually resilient ships needs a British aircraft carrier. Illustrious is favoured for repeatedly surviving difficult situations and continuing to operate. Her top speed by the end of the war is tentatively put at 25 knots, so the praise concerns endurance rather than undiminished performance. Victorious is also considered, although her large rebuild complicates the comparison of service records.

evidence.note: The fleet-selection discussion considers Illustrious and Victorious, qualifies Illustrious's late-war speed as possibly 25 knots, and mentions Victorious's large rebuild.

segments.summary: An imagined fleet selection favours Illustrious for continuing to serve through difficult operations, even with a possible late-war speed limit of 25 knots.

segments.title: Ark Royal's counter-flooding instructions
segments.body: Ark Royal's loss is attributed here partly to personnel who distrusted the instruction to counter-flood. They treated admitting water as the enemy's job and believed the manual must be wrong. The explanation specifically invokes a carrier's high metacentric height as the reason for the prescribed procedure. The practical lesson is that damage-control instincts can conflict with a ship's written stability instructions.

evidence.note: The account connects Ark Royal's loss with rejection of written counter-flooding instructions and explicitly invokes carrier metacentric height.

segments.summary: Ark Royal's loss is linked to a failure to follow written counter-flooding instructions when letting water aboard seemed instinctively wrong.

segments.title: Would a modern nuclear-powered battleship be practical?
segments.body: The viewer proposes a fast, nuclear-powered ship with escorts and large guns for long-range artillery support. Its armour would protect against 6-inch and smaller guns, while inexpensive defensive missiles would provide additional protection. The reply classifies that proposal as a battlecruiser or cruiser and leaves detailed feasibility to other discussions. Large guns, especially electromagnetic railguns, could return if their barrel metallurgy can meet the demands placed on them.

evidence.note: A battlecruiser or cruiser concept is offered in response to the modern battleship proposal, subject to the advanced-gun caveat.

segments.summary: The proposed nuclear-powered gun ship is classified as a battlecruiser or cruiser, while a return of advanced guns remains conditional on barrel metallurgy.
segments.question: Could a fast, escorted nuclear-powered battleship with long-range guns, armour against 6-inch and smaller guns, and missile defences be practical?
segments.answerShort: The proposal would be called a battlecruiser or cruiser. Advanced guns could return if barrel metallurgy improves, although no detailed feasibility assessment is offered.

segments.title: Choosing Texas among museum battleships
segments.body: A viewer waiting for Texas to return from dry dock prompts a personal preference for visiting her ahead of the other preserved American battleships. The Iowa-class ships remain attractive, and Ryan's work at New Jersey receives explicit praise. Texas comes first here because of her character, a subjective distinction from the personalities of the other ships.

evidence.note: A viewer shares a museum-visit wish rather than asking a question. The reply names Texas as a personal first choice, praises Ryan's work at New Jersey, and stresses ship character.

segments.summary: A personal preference puts USS Texas first for a museum visit, with praise for New Jersey's educational work.

segments.title: Battleships as shore-bombardment platforms
segments.body: Most US battleships did not exchange heavy-calibre fire with enemy capital ships, but their guns remained useful against targets ashore. The Iowa class later served effectively as shore-bombardment and cruise-missile platforms. A viewer argues that one Texas salvo delivered more high explosive than an early B-17 Flying Fortress's roughly four-ton bomb load. The reply accepts the broad comparison while stressing the battleship's drastically shorter range. It praises battleships as efficient bombardment platforms and allows heavy cruisers a role at shorter ranges. The salvo comparison remains qualitative here, without a calculation of the shells' explosive filling.

evidence.note: The exchange discusses Iowa-class bombardment and cruise-missile service, then compares a full Texas salvo with an early B-17's roughly four-ton bomb load.

segments.summary: Battleship shore bombardment is praised through the Iowa class's postwar service and a viewer's comparison of a Texas salvo with a B-17's bomb load.

segments.title: USS Texas with an occupation force in Mexico
segments.body: Sending USS Texas to Mexico as part of an American occupation force is treated as a politically blunt choice. The reaction jokes that somebody in the War Department threw away their copy of How to Win Friends and Influence People. The operation and its date are not identified in this exchange.

evidence.note: The conspicuous choice of Texas for the US Navy's occupation force in Mexico.

segments.summary: Sending USS Texas to Mexico as part of an American occupation force is described as a conspicuously blunt choice.

segments.title: USS Texas and an early talking picture at sea
segments.body: The question credits USS Texas with screening the first talking picture aboard a US Navy vessel and suggests Al Jolson's The Jazz Singer. The reply recalls having written down the title elsewhere, but can offer only a tentative memory that it was a western. Neither suggestion is confirmed, so the film remains unidentified in this exchange.

evidence.note: The viewer suggests Al Jolson's The Jazz Singer in a question about a 1927 screening. The reply repeatedly qualifies the recollection that it was a western and provides no confirmed title.

segments.summary: A viewer suggests The Jazz Singer as Texas's 1927 talking picture, while the reply tentatively recalls a western and cannot confirm the title.
segments.question: What talking picture did USS Texas screen aboard ship in 1927?
segments.answerShort: It may have been a western, but the title is not confirmed here.

segments.title: Warspite as a ballistic-missile submarine name
segments.body: Warspite had already been used for a nuclear attack submarine, or SSN, which is treated here as an acceptable continuation of the name. Applying it to a ballistic-missile submarine, or SSBN, feels more ominous. The reaction centres on a vessel that could strike the King's enemies anywhere in the world, tying the fighting name to the reach of the nuclear deterrent.

evidence.note: The response distinguishes the Warspite name on an SSN from its proposed use on an SSBN and expresses unease about the latter's global striking power.

segments.summary: Giving the Warspite name to an SSBN provokes unease about combining a famous fighting name with a submarine's global nuclear reach.

segments.title: Could Britain supply fuel for USS Arizona?
segments.body: A viewer suggests that Arizona's oil-fired boilers helped keep her in home waters during the First World War because Britain lacked fuel for her. The reply rejects the shortage argument, then turns mainly to British stockpiling since the 1920s and the Second World War. Naval fuel stores included bases such as Darwin, Singapore, and Alexandria, as well as dozens of sites in Britain. Ship fuel is distinguished from shortages affecting aviation and civilian motoring. Americans are said to have been surprised by the scale of British reserves even though some of the oil had been bought from them. The reserves described were measured in years of fleet operations, but that discussion does not establish why Arizona stayed in home waters.

evidence.note: A viewer raises oil supply as an explanation for Arizona's First World War deployment. The rebuttal moves into Second World War stocks, overseas and British storage sites, fuel categories, American surprise, and reserves measured in years.

segments.summary: A claim that Britain lacked fuel for oil-fired Arizona meets a rebuttal about naval oil reserves, with much of the explanation drawn from Second World War stockpiles.
segments.question: Did Britain's fuel situation prevent the oil-fired USS Arizona from operating with the Royal Navy during the First World War?
segments.answerShort: The reply rejects that explanation, arguing that Britain had substantial naval oil reserves. Much of its supporting discussion concerns the Second World War, and it does not settle Arizona's deployment history.

segments.title: Keeping years of naval fuel in reserve
segments.body: Britain continued taking deliveries of naval oil during the Second World War even while holding substantial reserves. Those imports are explained as a way to keep stocks topped up. The account maintains that ship-fuel reserves never fell below years of operations and were never at risk of exhaustion. A recalled comparison puts the stockpile higher in 1946 than in 1939, although the date and figures are offered from memory.

evidence.note: The explanation distinguishes continued fuel deliveries from a shortage, describes reserves remaining at years of operations, and tentatively recalls a 1946 versus 1939 stock comparison.

segments.summary: Continued oil deliveries are explained as replenishment of large British naval reserves, with a tentative recollection that stocks were larger in 1946 than in 1939.

segments.title: Tankers waiting for British naval oil storage
segments.body: A viewer connects the oil-fired Queen Elizabeth-class battleships with British preparations to stockpile fuel. The reply places that stockpiling before the First World War and says oilers were available in quantity. Shore storage could become the bottleneck. At several points, tankers waited in British waters while the Admiralty finished building space for their cargoes.

evidence.note: The exchange links Queen Elizabeth-class oil firing with prewar stockpiling, available oilers, and tankers waiting for storage construction. The exact spoken starting year is garbled as 19112 and is not asserted.

segments.summary: A discussion of oil-fired Queen Elizabeth-class battleships leads to prewar stockpiling and tankers waiting for the Admiralty to finish shore storage.
